newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Dhaka stocks turn bearish, SEC advice sends alarm.
newsitem.headline: Dhaka stocks turn bearish, SEC advice sends alarm.

text.p: The Bangladesh stock market's joy-ride ended as thousands of retail investors, jittery over a warning by regulators against speculating and trading in the kerb market, began selling, analysts said on Sunday.

The benchmark index of the Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) fell 4.44 percent or 90.03 points to close at 1,943.4 on Saturday. The index reached and all-time high of 2,005.24 on October 6. It was at 1,145.54 on August 1.
Brokers said share prices were falling sharply in early trading on Sunday amid selling pressure.

Market analysts said on Sunday that thousands of retail investors, who had propelled the market to newfound heights, had been selling heavily since Wednesday, when the SEC warned them to avoid the kerb market and steer clear of 24 companies it said where in the red.
The index dropped in successive days after the DSE limited share price movement to within 10 percent of the previous day's rate to discourage wild trading and halt speculation.
"No bid for any securities in a day shall be allowed in the Exchange in excess of +/- (plus or minus) 10 percent compared to the previous day's rate," it said in a statement on Thursday.
DSE officials said they implemented the new rule on Saturday on the advice of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the country's market watchdog.
There has been a mixed reaction to the steps, which came after record trading on the DSE by the retail investors, mostly unemployed or small savers.
"The warning came too late for the poor small investors. It should have come when the index crossed 1,000," said Redwanul Islam of Dastgir MD Adil & Co.
L.R. Sarkar, managing director of Prime Bank, which manages portfolio funds, said the steps would help the market to consolidate.
"The steps are very timely. I think this has prevented a major crash in the market," he said.
DSE Chairman Imtiyaz Husain told Reuters the SEC should have consulted trade and chamber bodies before taking such steps.

"It's a direct result of the government intervention in the operation of a self-regulatory body (the Dhaka Stock Exchange) which is not desired in a free market economy," Husain told the Daily Star in an interview published on Sunday.
But the SEC chief rejected the contention, saying the steps had been taken after the market turned extremely bullish without support by strong economic fundamentals of the companies.

"We had several meetings with the DSE, when we had tried to convince them (DSE officials)... We had to intervene. They should have done it as a self-regulatory body," SEC Chairman Haroonur Rashid told Reuters.
He said the DSE was refusing to take the steps despite the rapid changes in share prices.
"Things were going out of hand. We could not just sit idle," he said.
